title: Car rental management
alt: Actual car application showing synthetic vehicle and customer records
desc: A browser interface and REST API for managing vehicle and customer records.
built: Built a web application that connects a JavaScript interface to a Python API and relational database operations.
why: Everyday record management depends on clear workflows and consistent data. This prototype brings the interface, API and storage responsibilities together.
how: View vehicle and customer records in separate tables.
Create, update and delete records through asynchronous HTTP requests.
Use MySQL in the original application, or an explicit in-memory mode for a safe local demonstration.
demonstrates: Full-stack development, REST endpoints, relational data access and translating a record-management requirement into a usable interface.
caption: Actual Flask application, captured locally with synthetic records after the interface refresh.
result: Verified car and customer create, read, update and delete operations using Flask tests. Missing records return 404; invalid record fields are rejected.
limits: Academic prototype. The synthetic demo runs in memory and resets on restart. The original MySQL integration was inspected but not run against a live database. Authentication and deployment would need further work for real users.
technical: The existing data access classes remain in place for MySQL. An explicit DEMO_MODE selects a separate synthetic store. The homepage filename now matches case-sensitive filesystems; API error handling preserves 404 responses. Database initialization no longer drops an existing database.
run: Install requirements.txt. Set DEMO_MODE=1 in your local environment, then run python CarServer.py. Open http://127.0.0.1:5000. Run python -m unittest test_api.py.

title: Breast cancer classification
alt: Histogram of mean radius in the public Wisconsin dataset split by diagnosis label
desc: Explore a public dataset, compare classifiers and examine the limits of model evaluation.
built: Investigated the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset in a Python notebook, using exploration, feature selection and several classification methods.
why: A useful model starts with understanding the data and evaluating it carefully. This investigation shows the steps between a dataset and an interpretable comparison.
how: Explore class balance, feature relationships and correlations.
Split the data, scale training features and transform the held-out features.
Compare logistic regression, decision trees, random forests and additional classifiers, then discuss limitations.
demonstrates: Exploratory analysis, supervised learning, preprocessing, classifier comparison and critical interpretation of results.
caption: New presentation of authentic included data: mean-radius distributions by dataset label. This is descriptive analysis, not a diagnostic interface.
result: The corrected notebook executed all 42 code cells. Test scaling now uses training-set parameters, while cross-validation performs scaling inside each fold.
limits: Educational machine-learning investigation. No clinical use, independent validation or diagnostic capability is claimed. Feature selection remains exploratory; results on this single dataset do not establish real-world performance.
technical: Corrected Data/data.csv capitalization and removed deprecated np.bool usage. Added deterministic seeds to tree estimators, corrected test-set scaling and moved cross-validation preprocessing into pipelines. Regenerated notebook outputs are distinguished from historical narrative results.
run: Install requirements.txt and open PFDA Project 2.ipynb from the repository root in Jupyter. Run all cells in order.

title: Hotel booking prototype
alt: Actual hotel demo confirmation for two synthetic rooms over three nights, total 720 euro
desc: From dates and room selection to a server-calculated booking summary.
built: Built an Express and EJS hotel-booking prototype, then adapted the original college source into a safe, reproducible local demonstration.
why: A multi-step transaction should carry information reliably from one screen to the next. The project explores session state, validation and pricing across a booking journey.
how: Select a synthetic room type and quantity.
Review a server-calculated total on the confirmation page. No reservation or payment is made.
demonstrates: Server-rendered web development, session handling, input validation and turning a multi-step process into a working application.
caption: Actual Express/EJS confirmation screen. Synthetic example: two rooms × €120 × three nights = €720.
result: Browser-tested the complete dates → room → demo continuation → confirmation flow. Four automated tests verify date arithmetic, invalid dates, quantities and pricing. Dependency audit reported no known vulnerabilities at the time of review.
limits: Academic prototype with synthetic room prices. No live availability, real hotel affiliation, account system or payment integration. MySQL mode was inspected but not integration-tested. Original photographs were excluded because redistribution rights were unclear.
technical: Retained the original booking, room-selection and confirmation templates. Added missing-session guards and chronological date validation; totals are calculated server-side. Removed embedded API keys, SQL exports and broken CDN dependencies. The safe default uses synthetic room records and loopback binding.
run: Install Node.js. Run npm ci, npm test and npm start. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000. Use sample details only. Optional MySQL mode is documented in the repository.

title: Plant growth & statistics
alt: PlantGrowth box plots with every observed data point for control and two treatment groups
desc: Compare plant-growth treatments using visual exploration and statistical inference.
built: Analysed the PlantGrowth teaching dataset using distribution plots, assumption checks, group comparisons and follow-up tests.
why: Differences in averages can be misleading without considering variability. This project shows how visual evidence and statistical testing support a careful comparison.
how: Inspect 30 observations across a control and two treatment groups.
Explore distributions and check normality and variance assumptions.
Compare groups with t-tests, ANOVA, Tukey HSD and a non-parametric alternative.
demonstrates: Statistical reasoning, hypothesis testing, visual communication and explaining uncertainty around a decision.
caption: New visual presentation of all 30 original observations. Points show actual values; boxes summarize each group.
result: The project notebook executed all 18 code cells. The portfolio pairs a new chart of the source data with an original saved coursework plot.
limits: Small teaching dataset. Statistical significance alone does not establish practical importance or justify generalizing beyond the experiment. Independence depends on study design and cannot be proven by a plot.
technical: The source notebook includes Shapiro-Wilk checks, Q-Q plots, Levene’s test, one-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD and Kruskal-Wallis. Original references and methodology remain available alongside the code.
run: Install requirements.txt and Jupyter. Open project.ipynb from the repository root with PlantGrowth.csv alongside it.

title: Sorting algorithms, measured
alt: Measured median runtimes of five sorting algorithms across five input sizes on a logarithmic scale
desc: Implement five sorting algorithms and compare them using verified, repeatable measurements.
built: Implemented bubble, insertion, selection, quick and radix sorting, with visual explanations and benchmarking.
why: Two methods can produce the same answer while taking very different amounts of work. Correctness and measurement help make that trade-off visible.
how: Give each algorithm the same five seeded input samples at each size.
Time the sorting operation, then verify its output against Python’s sorted result.
Compare median runtimes across five sizes; preserve historical results separately.
demonstrates: Algorithmic thinking, regression testing, reproducible experimentation and interpreting performance evidence.
caption: New benchmark from 19 October 2026. Median of five runs per size; logarithmic time axis. Every measured result was checked for correctness.
result: Four regression test methods pass, covering empty inputs, duplicates, negative values for comparison sorts, random cases and radix-domain validation. The new benchmark verified 125 individual sorts.
limits: Timings depend on Python, machine load and hardware. Only random non-negative integers and sizes up to 1,000 were measured here. Quicksort’s worst-case recursion and other input distributions need separate investigation.
technical: benchmark_verified.py uses random.Random(40), time.perf_counter and median timing. Copies are prepared outside the timed region. The new CSV is separate from historical coursework data, whose aggregation needs further review before making performance claims.
run: Run python -m unittest test_algorithms.py, then python benchmark_verified.py. Review verified_timings.csv for the new measurements.

title: Iris dataset exploration
alt: Scatter plot of authentic Iris petal length and width with species labels
desc: Use summary statistics and visual exploration to reveal patterns in the Iris dataset.
built: Created a Python analysis script and notebook to summarize Iris measurements and explore relationships between features and species.
why: Before choosing a model, it helps to see how measurements vary and which features reveal useful structure. Clear exploratory analysis makes a dataset easier to understand.
how: Load the included Iris CSV and inspect its structure.
Calculate descriptive statistics and compare feature distributions.
Explore relationships with scatter plots, pair plots and correlations.
demonstrates: Data preparation, exploratory analysis, reproducible notebooks and selecting visuals that explain a pattern.
caption: New chart of the actual included Iris measurements. Species labels are provided in the dataset, not predictions.
result: The corrected notebook executed all 25 code cells. Case-sensitive CSV loading and numeric-only correlations now work in the tested environment.
limits: A small, well-known teaching dataset. Visible separation in petal measurements is an exploratory observation, not proof of performance on new datasets. The notebook’s classifier examples are educational extensions.
technical: Fixed Iris.csv to iris.csv for case-sensitive filesystems and restricted correlations to numeric columns for current pandas behavior. Seeded and stratified the training split. Original script, figures and sources remain available.
run: Install requirements.txt and open Project.ipynb from the repository root, or run analysis.py to produce the original summaries and histograms.
